title: Closure
body:
**A function plus the variables it captured from where it was defined, not from where it is
called.** That sentence is the whole concept, and every confusing thing about closures follows
from taking "where it was defined" literally.

A function in [[JavaScript]] can be created inside another function (see [[Nested Function]])
and then outlive it. When it does, the inner variables it referred to do not disappear with
the outer call; the inner function keeps them alive.

```js
function makeCounter() {
	let count = 0;                  // local to makeCounter
	return () => {                  // this function closes over count
		count = count + 1;
		return count;
	};
}

const next = makeCounter();
next();   // 1
next();   // 2
```

`makeCounter` has returned. Its stack frame is gone. `count` is still there, because `next`
holds it, and nothing else in the program can reach it. Two calls to `makeCounter()` produce
two independent counters with two independent `count`s.

## Why it exists

The rule that produces closures is [[Lexical]] scoping: what a name refers to is decided by
where the code is **written**, and the JS engine simply refuses to discard a binding that some
reachable function still refers to. Closures are not a feature that was added; they are what
you get for free once functions are values and scoping is lexical.

## What it buys you

| Use | How |
|---|---|
| Private state | the counter above: `count` is unreachable except through `next` |
| Callbacks that remember | a handler passed to `addEventListener` still sees the loop variable it was created with |
| Factory functions | `makeAdder(5)` returns a function that has captured `5` |
| Modules | the [[Immediately Invoked Function]] pattern, which is what [[Encapsulation]] in JS was before [[Module]]s existed |

The callback case is the one that actually bites, because it is why this is broken:

```js
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
	setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100);   // 3, 3, 3
}
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
	setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100);   // 0, 1, 2
}
```

`var` has one binding for the whole function, so all three closures captured the same `i` and
read it after the loop finished. `let` makes a fresh binding per iteration, so each closure
captured a different one. Closures capture **variables**, not values.

## What it is not

It is not a copy. If the captured variable changes later, the closure sees the new value; that
is the entire point of the `var` example above.

It is also not the same thing as [[Arrow Syntax]]'s treatment of [[This]], although both come
from lexical scoping. An arrow function has no `this` of its own and inherits the enclosing
one; that is lexical `this`, a separate rule that happens to rhyme with this one.

## Where it sits in the degree

Closures are the feature [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] names as the thing that makes JavaScript
usable functionally: they are what "a term keeps its free variables bound" means once you
leave [[Lambda Calculus]] and write real code. They are also the reason a
[[Call Back Function]] is useful at all rather than being a function that has forgotten its
context.

See [[JS Functions]], [[Objects]], and [[Variable Scope]] for the C++ side of the same
question.
